title: PreciseEdit: Strong Yet Stable Semantic Transport for One-Step Image Editing

paper.title: PreciseEdit: Strong Yet Stable Semantic Transport for One-Step Image Editing
paper.abstract: Abstract. Recent one-step text-to-image (T2I) models enable efficient image synthesis, opening up new possibilities for interactive Web-based image editing. However, existing one-step editing methods often construct a global transport field through simple vector operations between conditional predictions. While such strong transport can effectively drive the image toward the target semantics, it may be released along unreliable directions or over non-edited regions, leading to structural distortions within the editing region and background drift elsewhere. More importantly, stabilizing the editing process through global smoothing or uniformly weakening the transport field often makes large semantic changes overly conservative. In this work, we revisit one-step image editing from the perspective of the tension between semantic strength and transport stability, and identify a key insight: strong semantic transport is not inherently unstable. What matters is whether it is applied along reliable directions and at reliable spatial locations. Motivated by this insight, we introduce PreciseEdit, a model-agnostic, training-free and inversion-free one-step editing framework that strengthens target-semantic alignment while preserving background fidelity and structural consistency. We further propose a dual-noise-scale role decomposition strategy: a higher-noise scale produces the strong target-directed transport used for actual editing, whereas a lower-noise scale jointly serves as a probe for directional agreement and spatial structure. Extensive experiments on PIE-Bench demonstrate that PreciseEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance and effectiveness on various editing tasks.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Modern Web platforms support visual creation and editing across social media, e-commerce, and online design tools, where users iteratively revise uploaded images through natural-language instructions. Recent one-step text-to-image (T2I) models, including SD-Turbo ( Sauer et al., 2024 ) , SwiftBrush-v2 ( Dao et al., 2024 ) , and InstaFlow ( Liu et al., 2024 ) , substantially reduce generation latency, making interactive image creation increasingly practical. These advances motivate real-time text-guided editing for Web-based visual authoring, which requires low latency, strong semantic transformations within intended editing regions, and reliable preservation of non-edited content across successive edits. However, efficient one-step editing that enables strong semantic transformations while preserving high fidelity remains challenging. Some fast editors rely on trained inversion networks or explicit inversion ( Nguyen et al., 2025 ; Gong et al., 2025 ) , while training-free and inversion-free approaches construct editing directions directly from conditional predictions ( Kulikov et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2024 ) . Yet, compressing semantic transformation into a single update creates a pronounced strength–stability dilemma. ChordEdit ( Lu et al., 2026 ) stabilizes editing through temporal smoothing and a low-energy field but can under-realize large semantic changes, whereas the concurrent work WhereEdit ( Hu et al., 2026 ) enables stronger spatially constrained editing but still relies on relatively coarse localization and an additional U-Net evaluation. Despite their different formulations, these approaches expose two prominent drawbacks. First, globally weakening transport improves preservation but limits semantic transformations. Second, stronger transport improves target-semantic alignment but can cause background drift or structural distortion when applied unreliably. These issues naturally lead us to reconsider the current paradigm and pose a critical question: Can strong semantic transport remain stable in one-step image editing? To address this question, we begin by analyzing different semantic transport regimes and the factors governing their stability. Fig. 1 reveals that, with the official GT masks from PIE-Bench ( Ju et al., 2024 ) , both ChordEdit and WhereEdit substantially improve non-edited-region fidelity, underscoring the importance of reliable spatial localization. Meanwhile, ChordEdit remains conservative even with accurate spatial guidance, whereas the stronger transport of WhereEdit achieves larger semantic changes but can still affect non-target regions. These observations suggest that strong semantic transport is not inherently unstable; reliable spatial localization is critical to its stability. Moreover, because a one-step update offers no later opportunity to correct misdirected transport, directional reliability is equally important. This insight naturally motivates a selective-release editing strategy: construct a strong transport field directed toward the target semantics, but release it only at reliable spatial locations and along reliable directions. Guided by this principle, we propose PreciseEdit, a training-free and inversion-free framework that explicitly regulates strong semantic transport through spatial and directional reliability. Implementing this idea, however, raises two critical challenges: (1) How to precisely and efficiently identify where to edit? and (2) How to keep strong semantic transport stable? For Challenge 1 , we propose PreciseMask, a structure-aware spatial gating mechanism that combines lower-noise cross-attention semantics with self-attention structural affinity to identify reliable edit regions. PreciseMask reuses attention from the main U-Net evaluation, requiring neither external segmentation nor additional U-Net evaluations. For Challenge 2 , we introduce Strong Conditional Transport (SCT), which augments source-to-target conditional contrast with anchor-relative target attraction to provide sufficient semantic modification. Cross-scale directional agreement suppresses transport directions inconsistent with a lower-noise reference, while PreciseMask provides complementary spatial regulation. Together, they enable strong transport to remain stable within a single-step update. To effectively integrate these two modules, we propose a dual-noise-scale role decomposition strategy. The higher-noise scale provides strong semantic transport, while the lower-noise scale supplies spatial evidence and directional references. This complementary strategy couples semantic strength with transport stability within a unified one-step framework. Figure 2. Quality–efficiency comparison on PIE-Bench ( Ju et al., 2024 ) . Each point represents an image-editing method. The horizontal axis reports runtime, while the vertical axes report background fidelity measured by PSNR-Unedit (top) and target-semantic alignment measured by CLIP-Edited (bottom) ( Radford et al., 2021 ) . Marker size indicates peak VRAM usage. PreciseEdit achieves a favorable balance among background preservation, semantic alignment, and inference efficiency. Runtime is shown on the horizontal axis, PSNR-Unedit and CLIP-Edited are shown on the vertical axes, and marker size represents peak VRAM usage. The main contributions can be summarized as follows: (1) We propose PreciseMask, fusing lower-noise cross- and self-attention for precise, structure-aware edit localization without an external segmenter or extra U-Net evaluations. (2) We introduce Strong Conditional Transport (SCT) to strengthen target-directed transport, with cross-scale directional agreement suppressing unreliable directions. (3) We propose a dual-noise-scale strategy that leverages the complementary properties of the two noise scales to decouple transport-field construction from spatial localization, yielding leading PIE-Bench results across backbones.

sections.heading: 2.1. Text-Guided Editing with Diffusion/Flow Models
sections.text: Diffusion and latent-diffusion models established a strong foundation for text-guided visual generation and editing ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Meng et al., 2022 ; Hertz et al., 2023 ) . Early real-image editors commonly rely on inversion, attention control, guidance, or latent optimization ( Mokady et al., 2023 ; Wallace et al., 2023 ; Kawar et al., 2023 ; Dong et al., 2023 ; Tumanyan et al., 2023 ; Han et al., 2024 ) . Methods such as PnP ( Tumanyan et al., 2023 ) and ProxEdit ( Han et al., 2024 ) achieve high-quality editing but require iterative inversion and multi-step sampling. Recent distilled and consistency-based generators ( Song et al., 2023 ; Nguyen and Tran, 2024 ; Yin et al., 2024b ; Yin et al., 2024a ; Peng et al., 2026 ; Geng et al., 2025 ) , including SD-Turbo ( Sauer et al., 2024 ) , InstaFlow ( Liu et al., 2024 ) , and SwiftBrush-v2 ( Dao et al., 2024 ) , enable one- or few-step generation, but their accelerated dynamics make precise editing more challenging.

sections.heading: 2.2. Training-Free and Inversion-Free Editing
sections.text: To improve efficiency, recent studies avoid per-image inversion and additional model training ( Kulikov et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . FlowEdit ( Kulikov et al., 2025 ) and InfEdit ( Xu et al., 2024 ) provide inversion-free editing but still rely on iterative or few-step updates. Fast editors such as TurboEdit ( Deutch et al., 2024 ) , invertible consistency distillation ( Starodubcev et al., 2024 ) , and SwiftEdit ( Nguyen et al., 2025 ) reduce the sampling cost, yet compressing semantic transformation into very few updates makes fidelity and edit strength harder to balance. ChordEdit ( Lu et al., 2026 ) stabilizes one-step transport through a low-energy control field, but the resulting conservative transport can limit large semantic changes.

sections.heading: 2.3. Mask-Guided Controlled Image Editing
sections.text: Spatial controllability is central to precise editing. Prior work localizes modifications with explicit masks ( Avrahami et al., 2022 ; Couairon et al., 2023 ; Cao et al., 2023 ) or internal attention/features ( Hertz et al., 2023 ; Mao et al., 2024 ; Tang et al., 2024 ; Soni et al., 2025 ) . LIME ( Simsar et al., 2025 ) combines intermediate features and cross-attention, LayerEdit ( Fu et al., 2026 ) decomposes objects, and WhereEdit ( Hu et al., 2026 ) aggregates cross-attention to estimate editable regions. These approaches may require inversion, iterative sampling, external segmentation, or extra localization/optimization, limiting one-step efficiency. PreciseEdit instead reuses lower-noise cross- and self-attention with graph refinement, requiring no external segmenter, learnable parameters, or additional U-Net evaluation for mask generation.

sections.heading: 3. Method
sections.text: We propose PreciseEdit, a training-free and inversion-free framework for one-step image editing. PreciseEdit separates semantic strength from stability: the higher-noise scale provides the primary SCT, while the lower-noise scale supplies both a directional reference and attention-derived spatial support. The final update combines the primary SCT, cross-scale directional modulation, and continuous PreciseMask gating in latent space. Figure 3. Comparison of editing transport properties. (a) Multi-step editing: iterative updates progressively correct the trajectory toward the target. (b) Naive one-step editing: a single conditional residual may provide insufficient target attraction and miss the desired target. (c) ChordEdit ( Lu et al., 2026 ) : temporal smoothing produces a stable low-energy transport field, but can lead to conservative semantic changes. (d) SCT (Ours): anchor-relative target attraction strengthens target-directed transport, while cross-scale directional agreement suppresses unreliable directions for stable one-step editing. Conceptual comparison of multi-step editing, naive one-step editing, ChordEdit, and the proposed SCT with higher- and lower-noise scales.

sections.heading: 3.2.1. Anchor-Relative Target Attraction
sections.text: Multi-step editing can correct early errors through iterative feedback, whereas one-step editing must realize sufficiently large semantic changes in a single update. We therefore seek a transport that is explicitly target-directed and adaptive to the discrepancy between the current anchor and the target-conditioned prediction. At noise scale t t , subtracting the source-conditioned prediction from the target-conditioned prediction gives the naive conditional residual: (4) R n ​ a ​ i ​ v ​ e ​ ( t , x ) = μ ^ t ​ a ​ r ​ ( t , x ) − μ ^ s ​ r ​ c ​ ( t , x ) . R_{naive}(t,x)=\widehat{\mu}_{tar}(t,x)-\widehat{\mu}_{src}(t,x). R n ​ a ​ i ​ v ​ e R_{naive} captures the source-to-target conditional contrast under the same noisy observation, but it remains a prediction-to-prediction difference and does not explicitly encode displacement from the current anchor x x to the target-conditioned reference. Uniformly scaling this residual changes only its magnitude. We therefore introduce an anchor-relative target attraction: (5) a ⁡ ( t , x ) = k ⁡ [ μ ^ t ​ a ​ r ​ ( t , x ) − x ] . a(t,x)=k\left[\widehat{\mu}_{tar}(t,x)-x\right]. Here k ≥ 0 k\geq 0 balances this attraction against the conditional residual. The attraction a ⁡ ( t , x ) a(t,x) points directly from x x toward the target-conditioned clean-latent prediction, while its magnitude reflects the remaining target discrepancy. It vanishes when the two coincide. Combining the conditional residual and anchor-relative target attraction yields Strong Conditional Transport (SCT): (6) u S ​ C ​ T ​ ( t , x ) = R n ​ a ​ i ​ v ​ e ​ ( t , x ) + a ⁡ ( t , x ) . u^{SCT}(t,x)=R_{naive}(t,x)+a(t,x). SCT therefore preserves the source-to-target conditional contrast while restoring explicit target reachability. Unlike scalar amplification of R n ​ a ​ i ​ v ​ e R_{naive} , its additional transport strength adapts jointly to the current anchor and target-conditioned prediction.

sections.heading: 3.3. PreciseMask
sections.text: Directional agreement determines whether the primary SCT is trustworthy, but not where it should act. We therefore use edit support to quantify spatial evidence for applying the requested latent update. PreciseMask is constructed entirely at the lower-noise scale t l t_{l} by reusing cross- and self-attention from the source- and target-conditioned branches. As illustrated in Fig. 4 , branch-specific cross-attention produces semantic-support seeds, confidence-weighted self-attention graph-Laplacian refinement propagates them along coherent visual structures, and adaptive soft gating converts the refined support into PreciseMask.

sections.heading: 4.1. Experimental Setup
sections.text: Dataset and evaluation metrics. We conduct our empirical evaluation on PIE-Bench ( Ju et al., 2024 ) , a standard benchmark for instruction-based image editing on 512 × 512 512\times 512 images. The benchmark contains 700 samples distributed across 10 distinct editing categories, with each sample providing a source image, source and target textual prompts, blend word, and a GT mask specifying the editing region. We assess performance along two complementary axes: background fidelity and semantic alignment. Background fidelity is measured using PSNR, MSE, and LPIPS on the non-edited regions, while semantic alignment is evaluated using CLIP-Whole and CLIP-Edited ( Radford et al., 2021 ) for the entire image and edited region, respectively. Implementation details. Code will be made publicly available upon acceptance. Our default backbone is SD-Turbo ( Sauer et al., 2024 ) , evaluated in FP32 on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU with 24 GB of memory, using one shared Gaussian noise sample ( n = 1 n=1 ). We set the higher-noise scale to t h = 0.90 t_{h}=0.90 , the lower-noise scale to t l = 0.35 t_{l}=0.35 , and the target-conditioned refinement scale to t r = 0.30 t_{r}=0.30 . The SCT attraction coefficient is k = 2.0 k=2.0 , and the latent step size is 1.0 1.0 . One batched U-Net evaluation processes the source- and target-conditioned branches at both noise scales, followed by one target-only evaluation for proximal refinement.

sections.heading: 4.2. Comparison with Prior Methods
sections.text: Quantitative Results. Table 1 compares preservation, semantic alignment, and efficiency under the unified PIE-Bench protocol. PreciseEdit reaches 24.37 dB PSNR-Unedit and 23.36 CLIP-Edited, improving over ChordEdit ( Lu et al., 2026 ) by 1.73 dB and 1.20, respectively, and over WhereEdit ( Hu et al., 2026 ) by 0.41 dB and 0.70. PreciseMask recovers 9.81 dB PSNR-Unedit while retaining 23.36 CLIP-Edited, directly supporting selective release. The GT-guided variant further reaches 27.34 PSNR-Unedit and 23.90 CLIP-Edited, indicating that more accurate spatial support remains meaningful headroom. Qualitative Results. Figure 5 shows the same trend across diverse edit types. Existing methods often either under-realize the target concept or alter unrelated appearance and geometry. This behavior appears in both global edits, where background changes can leak into foreground structure, and localized object or attribute edits, where excessive transport can disturb shape or identity. PreciseEdit more consistently changes the requested concept while retaining source composition, object structure, and non-edited appearance. Taken together, these results suggest that the key advantage is not maximizing preservation or edit strength in isolation, but retaining strong target-directed transport while controlling its directional and spatial reliability. We next examine these factors separately.

sections.heading: 5. Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we revisited one-step image editing through the tension between semantic strength and transport reliability. Instead of globally suppressing strong transport, we proposed PreciseEdit, a training- and inversion-free framework that selectively trusts it according to directional and spatial reliability. Our dual-noise-scale design uses a higher-noise scale to construct Strong Conditional Transport, while a lower-noise scale provides directional calibration and structured spatial support through PreciseMask. By combining cross-attention semantic seeds, self-attention graph-Laplacian refinement, and adaptive soft gating, PreciseEdit localizes strong semantic changes while preserving irrelevant regions. Extensive experiments on PIE-Bench ( Ju et al., 2024 ) demonstrate that PreciseEdit achieves a favorable fidelity–editability Pareto balance while retaining low latency and memory usage. Its consistent gains across multiple one-step backbones further support the generality of the proposed formulation. We hope that the perspective of separating semantic strength from reliability will provide a useful foundation for efficient, precise, and controllable image editing.

Recent one-step text-to-image (T2I) models enable efficient image synthesis, opening up new possibilities for interactive Web-based image editing. However, existing one-step editing methods often construct a global transport field through simple vector operations between conditional predictions. While such strong transport can effectively drive the image toward the target semantics, it may be released along unreliable directions or over non-edited regions, leading to structural distortions within the editing region and background drift elsewhere. More importantly, stabilizing the editing process through global smoothing or uniformly weakening the transport field often makes large semantic changes overly conservative. In this work, we revisit one-step image editing from the perspective of the tension between semantic strength and transport stability, and identify a key insight: strong semantic transport is not inherently unstable. What matters is whether it is applied along reliable directions and at reliable spatial locations. Motivated by this insight, we introduce PreciseEdit, a model-agnostic, training-free and inversion-free one-step editing framework that strengthens target-semantic alignment while preserving background fidelity and structural consistency. We further propose a dual-noise-scale role decomposition strategy: a higher-noise scale produces the strong target-directed transport used for actual editing, whereas a lower-noise scale jointly serves as a probe for directional agreement and spatial structure. Extensive experiments on PIE-Bench demonstrate that PreciseEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance and effectiveness on various editing tasks. The second row illustrates the strength–stability dilemma in one-step editing: ChordEdit ( Lu et al., 2026 ) remains conservative even with accurate spatial guidance, whereas the stronger transport of WhereEdit ( Hu et al., 2026 ) achieves larger semantic changes but may affect non-target regions, raising our second challenge. Introduction Modern Web platforms support visual creation and editing across social media, e-commerce, and online design tools, where users iteratively revise uploaded images through natural-language instructions. Recent one-step text-to-image (T2I) models, including SD-Turbo ( Sauer et al., 2024 ) , SwiftBrush-v2 ( Dao et al., 2024 ) , and InstaFlow ( Liu et al., 2024 ) , substantially reduce generation latency, making interactive image creation increasingly practical. These advances motivate real-time text-guided editing for Web-based visual authoring, which requires low latency, strong semantic transformations within intended editing regions, and reliable preservation of non-edited content across successive edits. However, efficient one-step editing that enables strong semantic transformations while preserving high fidelity remains challenging. Some fast editors rely on trained inversion networks or explicit inversion ( Nguyen et al., 2025 ; Gong et al., 2025 ) , while training-free and inversion-free approaches construct editing directions directly from conditional predictions ( Kulikov et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2024 ) . Yet, compressing semantic transformation into a single update creates a pronounced strength–stability dilemma. ChordEdit ( Lu et al., 2026 ) stabilizes editing through temporal smoothing and a low-energy field but can under-realize large semantic changes, whereas the concurrent work WhereEdit ( Hu et al., 2026 ) enables stronger spatially constrained editing but still relies on relatively coarse localization and an additional U-Net evaluation. Despite their different formulations, these approaches expose two prominent drawbacks. First, globally weakening transport improves preservation but limits semantic transformations. Second, stronger transport improves target-semantic alignment but can cause background drift or structural distortion when applied unreliably. These issues naturally lead us to reconsider the current paradigm and pose a critical question: Can strong semantic transport remain stable in one-step image editing? To address this question, we begin by analyzing different semantic transport regimes and the factors governing their stability. Fig. 1 reveals that, with the official GT masks from PIE-Bench ( Ju et al., 2024 ) , both ChordEdit and WhereEdit substantially improve non-edited-region fidelity, underscoring the importance of reliable spatial localization. Meanwhile, ChordEdit remains conservative even with accurate spatial guidance, whereas the stronger transport of WhereEdit achieves larger semantic changes but can still affect non-target regions. These observations suggest that strong semantic transport is not inherently unstable; reliable spatial localization is critical to its stability. Moreover, because a one-step update offers no later opportunity to correct misdirected transport, directional reliability is equally important. This insight naturally motivates a selective-release editing strategy: construct a strong transport field directed toward the target semantics, but release it only at reliable spatial locations and along reliable directions. Guided by this principle, we propose PreciseEdit, a training-free and inversion-free framework that explicitly regulates strong semantic transport through spatial and directional reliability. Implementing this idea, however, raises two critical challenges: (1) How to precisely and efficiently identify where to edit? and (2) How to keep strong semantic transport stable? For Challenge 1 , we propose PreciseMask, a structure-aware spatial gating mechanism that combines lower-noise cross-attention semantics with self-attention structural affinity to identify reliable edit regions. PreciseMask reuses attention from the main U-Net evaluation, requiring neither external segmentation nor additional U-Net evaluations. For Challenge 2 , we introduce Strong Conditional Transport (SCT), which augments source-to-target conditional contrast with anchor-relative target attraction to provide sufficient semantic modification. Cross-scale directional agreement suppresses transport directions inconsistent with a lower-noise reference, while PreciseMask provides complementary spatial regulation. Together, they enable strong transport to remain stable within a single-step update. To effectively integrate these two modules, we propose a dual-noise-scale role decomposition strategy. The higher-noise scale provides strong semantic transport, while the lower-noise scale supplies spatial evidence and directional references. This complementary strategy couples semantic strength with transport stability within a unified one-step framework. Figure 2. Quality–efficiency comparison on PIE-Bench ( Ju et al., 2024 ) . The horizontal axis reports runtime, while the vertical axes report background fidelity measured by PSNR-Unedit (top) and target-semantic alignment measured by CLIP-Edited (bottom) ( Radford et al., 2021 ) . The main contributions can be summarized as follows: (1) We propose PreciseMask, fusing lower-noise cross- and self-attention for precise, structure-aware edit localization without an external segmenter or extra U-Net evaluations. (2) We introduce Strong Conditional Transport (SCT) to strengthen target-directed transport, with cross-scale directional agreement suppressing unreliable directions. (3) We propose a dual-noise-scale strategy that leverages the complementary properties of the two noise scales to decouple transport-field construction from spatial localization, yielding leading PIE-Bench results across backbones. 2. Related Work 2.1. Text-Guided Editing with Diffusion/Flow Models Diffusion and latent-diffusion models established a strong foundation for text-guided visual generation and editing ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Meng et al., 2022 ; Hertz et al., 2023 ) . Early real-image editors commonly rely on inversion, attention control, guidance, or latent optimization ( Mokady et al., 2023 ; Wallace et al., 2023 ; Kawar et al., 2023 ; Dong et al., 2023 ; Tumanyan et al., 2023 ; Han et al., 2024 ) . Methods such as PnP ( Tumanyan et al., 2023 ) and ProxEdit ( Han et al., 2024 ) achieve high-quality editing but require iterative inversion and multi-step sampling. Recent distilled and consistency-based generators ( Song et al., 2023 ; Nguyen and Tran, 2024 ; Yin et al., 2024b ; Yin et al., 2024a ; Peng et al., 2026 ; Geng et al., 2025 ) , including SD-Turbo ( Sauer et al., 2024 ) , InstaFlow ( Liu et al., 2024 ) , and SwiftBrush-v2 ( Dao et al., 2024 ) , enable one- or few-step generation, but their accelerated dynamics make precise editing more challenging. 2.2. Training-Free and Inversion-Free Editing To improve efficiency, recent studies avoid per-image inversion and additional model training ( Kulikov et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . FlowEdit ( Kulikov et al., 2025 ) and InfEdit ( Xu et al., 2024 ) provide inversion-free editing but still rely on iterative or few-step updates. Fast editors such as TurboEdit ( Deutch et al., 2024 ) , invertible consistency distillation ( Starodubcev et al., 2024 ) , and SwiftEdit ( Nguyen et al., 2025 ) reduce the sampling cost, yet compressing semantic transformation into very few updates makes fidelity and edit strength harder to balance. ChordEdit ( Lu et al., 2026 ) stabilizes one-step transport through a low-energy control field, but the resulting conservative transport can limit large semantic changes. 2.3. Mask-Guided Controlled Image Editing Spatial controllability is central to precise editing. Prior work localizes modifications with explicit masks ( Avrahami et al., 2022 ; Couairon et al., 2023 ; Cao et al., 2023 ) or internal attention/features ( Hertz et al., 2023 ; Mao et al., 2024 ; Tang et al., 2024 ; Soni et al., 2025 ) . LIME ( Simsar et al., 2025 ) combines intermediate features and cross-attention, LayerEdit ( Fu et al., 2026 ) decomposes objects, and WhereEdit ( Hu et al., 2026 ) aggregates cross-attention to estimate editable regions. These approaches may require inversion, iterative sampling, external segmentation, or extra localization/optimization, limiting one-step efficiency. PreciseEdit instead reuses lower-noise cross- and self-attention with graph refinement, requiring no external segmenter, learnable parameters, or additional U-Net evaluation for mask generation. 3. PreciseEdit separates semantic strength from stability: the higher-noise scale provides the primary SCT, while the lower-noise scale supplies both a directional reference and attention-derived spatial support. We conduct our empirical evaluation on PIE-Bench ( Ju et al., 2024 ) , a standard benchmark for instruction-based image editing on 512 × 512 512\times 512 images. The benchmark contains 700 samples distributed across 10 distinct editing categories, with each sample providing a source image, source and target textual prompts, blend word, and a GT mask specifying the editing region. We assess performance along two complementary axes: background fidelity and semantic alignment. Background fidelity is measured using PSNR, MSE, and LPIPS on the non-edited regions, while semantic alignment is evaluated using CLIP-Whole and CLIP-Edited ( Radford et al., 2021 ) for the entire image and edited region, respectively. Implementation details. Code will be made publicly available upon acceptance. Our default backbone is SD-Turbo ( Sauer et al., 2024 ) , evaluated in FP32 on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU with 24 GB of memory, using one shared Gaussian noise sample ( n = 1 n=1 ). We set the higher-noise scale to t h = 0.90 t_{h}=0.90 , the lower-noise scale to t l = 0.35 t_{l}=0.35 , and the target-conditioned refinement scale to t r = 0.30 t_{r}=0.30 . The SCT attraction coefficient is k = 2.0 k=2.0 , and the latent step size is 1.0 1.0 . One batched U-Net evaluation processes the source- and target-conditioned branches at both noise scales, followed by one target-only evaluation for proximal refinement. 4.2.
